title: The good of all
hookLine: the year ends where every Ardas ends, asking good for everyone

cards: Amritsar, the 1700s, a spring morning at Vaisakhi. Riders come in from every direction: bands that spend the rest of the year scattered, sometimes quarreling, often hunted.
For a few days they camp side by side, sit together before the Guru Granth Sahib, and decide things as one. That gathering, which you met on day 289, was the Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat, everyone.
Everyone who belonged. Every Ardas still ends with that word, but there it reaches far past the riders camped at Amritsar.

teach.b: On day 251 you took the Ardas's last line apart: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits through the Name, and, by your will, the good of all. Today, one word, because you've now met it twice.

teach.h: SARBAT DA BHALA: THE WHOLE OF EVERYTHING.
teach.b: In the Sarbat Khalsa, it meant the whole Khalsa: every band, every leader, everyone who belonged, gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Ardas, it stretches past every border. Not the whole Khalsa.
The whole of everything. Sarbat da bhala: the good of all, full stop. Think who says it.
This year's path walked through a community hunted in the forests, massacred in 1746 and again in 1762, turned away from a harbor in 1914, attacked in its holiest place and in its own neighborhoods.
The Ardas remembers much of that. And it doesn't end with protect our own, or defeat our enemies.

teach.h: A HURT PEOPLE ASKS GOOD FOR ALL.
teach.b: It ends by asking good for everyone, and Sikh teachers often say plainly that this includes the people who did the hurting.
It grows out of what the Gurus taught: one light in every person; no enemy and no stranger, as Guru Arjan sings on Ang 1299.

teach.h: BY YOUR WILL, IN YOUR WAY.
teach.b: And notice tere bhane, by your will.
The prayer doesn't tell God what everyone's good should look like. It asks, and leaves the shape of it to the Giver.
A fitting place to stand at the end of a year of stories, practices, the Japji and the depths: a prayer whose last word reaches past the people saying it.

how: Every Ardas, in every gurdwara and at home, ends with the line asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, before the congregation calls out the jaikara.

o: a sweet offering shared after prayer
the Guru's blessing on one family

games.q: the last line of the Ardas — tap the pairs.

s: the Ardas ends by asking protection for Sikhs alone
it ends by asking the good of everyone: sarbat da bhala.
the last line leaves the shape of everyone's good to God's will
tere bhane: by your will, in your way.
sarbat means the same circle in the Sarbat Khalsa and in the Ardas
in the Sarbat Khalsa it meant the whole Khalsa; in the Ardas's last line, everyone.

games.q: a community has been hurt again and again. its daily prayer is ending. what's the very last thing it asks for?
o: that it be kept safe from outsiders.
games.why: every Ardas ends with sarbat da bhala: by your will, may all be well.

practice: Wish good for three people from this year: first someone who taught you something, in any way at all; then someone on the other side of a disagreement you're in, at home, at work or in the news, even a little; last, someone far away whose story you heard on this path and will never meet.
Wish each well, in your own words or none. If you pray, hold all three in your prayer; if not, just hold them.

wordCard.voice: Sarbat. Everyone, the whole of everything — in sarbat da bhala, the last words of every Ardas, asking good for all.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sarbat da bhala, the good of all; the last words of every Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: for everyone, not just us. Sarbat da bhala. Day three hundred thirty.
